reason: Block and schema payloads are base64 Arrow IPC. Java Arrow and arrow-rs may pad buffers differently, so diff.py compares the decoded schema and rows, not the bytes. pyarrow is not installed on this host, so java/ArrowDecode (Java Arrow 18.3) decodes both sides; Athena reads the payloads with Java Arrow too. TODO: decode with pyarrow when it is installed, so the decoder shares no code with the Java side.

Spilled blocks and the export schema sidecar are Arrow IPC written to the S3 stub. They are decoded like inline blocks, using the schema of the RemoteReadRecordsResponse, and the byte size is dropped because it depends on buffer padding.
BlockAllocatorImpl() names each allocator with a random UUID, and every serialized block carries that id.
MetadataHandler.makeSpillLocation uses UUID.randomUUID() as the split id at the end of the spill key.

MetadataHandler.makeEncryptionKey draws a random AES key for every split when spill encryption is on, and RemoteReadRecordsResponse echoes the random key from the request. Only the decoded length is compared.
The nonce is random for the same reason as the key. Only the decoded length is compared.
GetSplitsResponse keeps the splits in a HashSet and Split.hashCode includes the random spill key, so the JSON order changes from run to run.
JdbcMetadataHandler.doGetTable builds partition columns with Collectors.toSet(), so the order is a hash order and not part of the contract.

When the ReadRecordsRequest split carries an encryptionKey, S3BlockSpiller writes each block as AES-GCM ciphertext. The key and nonce come from the request, and CorpusGen draws a new random key on every run, so the ciphertext never repeats. diff.py passes the split key and nonce to java/ArrowDecode, which decrypts each spilled object and compares the plaintext block. A block that fails to decrypt shows up as a decodeError.

S3BlockSpiller.makeSpillLocation (S3BlockSpiller.java:494) numbers each block with spillNumber.getAndIncrement() when a spill thread writes it, so with two spill threads the block that gets .0 depends on thread timing. The suffix is masked, and the count of distinct objects in the S3 stub still checks that every block got its own key.
The spilled object paths carry the same thread-order block number as the remoteBlocks keys.
With the block number masked, the S3 objects are sorted by their decoded content, so the same set of blocks compares equal whatever order the spill threads finished in.
S3BlockSpiller records spill locations from two async spill threads in completion order.
QueryStatusChecker polls Athena from a background thread after one second, so whether the call happens depends on how long the read takes.
